podcast.title: Greenwich Village Figure
podcast.body: Moondog was a street musician who was part of the bohemian scene in Greenwich Village in the early 1960s, alongside poets like Allen Ginsberg and performers like Tiny Tim. "people like the poet Alan Ginsburg, the street musician Moondog, and tiny Tim"

podcast.title: Later Career and Influence
podcast.body: Moondog was taken seriously as a performer and composer, eventually securing a recording contract for multiple albums. He married, started a family, and returned to Carnegie Hall in 1989 to conduct a performance of his own works. He later moved to Europe, where he died of heart failure in 1999 at age 83. His life and music were inspirational to various artists, from hippies to bands important to the creation of Trip Hop. "Moon Dog eventually found his way to Europe where he died of heart failure in 1999 at the age of 83."

srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 1

podcast.title: Lawsuit Against Allan Freed
podcast.body: Moondog, incensed by disc jockey Allan Freed's unauthorized use of his "Moon Dog" moniker and "Moon Dog Symphony" as a radio show theme, sued Freed with the help of big band leader Benny Goodman. Moondog won the lawsuit, securing $6,000 in damages and a promise that Freed would never use the name "Moon Dog" again, directly influencing Freed's adoption of "rock and roll" as a descriptive term for the new music. "The actual Moon Dog was, as you might guess, incensed, so with the help of big band leader Benny Goodman, he sued Alan Fried, and he won six thousand dollars in damages."

podcast.title: Street Performer and Composer
podcast.body: Louis Hardin Jr., known as Moondog, was a homeless, six-foot, blind New York street performer. He dressed in a Viking costume and often stood silently banging a drum outside Carnegie Hall, composing music and releasing records under the name Moon Dog. His striking appearance and musical talent attracted attention from famous composers and conductors. "Lewis Harden Jr., a homeless six-foot blind New York street performer who dressed up in a Viking costume and could often be found outside the stage door of Carnegie Hall, standing silently and banging a drum."

xref.title: Coining the Term "Rock and Roll"
xref.body: Freed famously started referring to the music he played on his radio show as "Rock and Roll." This change in terminology occurred after a New York street musician, who claimed prior usage of the name "Moondog," threatened legal action. One theory suggests Freed derived the term from the 1951 recording "60 Minute Man" by Billy Ward and the Dominoes, which included the lyric "I rock them, roll them all night long," known as African American slang for sexual intercourse, a meaning Freed was likely aware of. "Fried also famously eventually started calling the music he played on his radio show, Rock and Roll."

xref.title: Forced Renaming and Coining "Rock and Roll"
xref.body: After losing a lawsuit to the original Moondog (Louis Hardin Jr.), Allan Freed was forced to stop using the "Moon Dog" moniker. Needing to revamp his image and find a new catchphrase, he decided to use "rock and roll," an African-American slang phrase for sex. This term was understood by the youth but not by parents, thus becoming the widely adopted descriptor for the new type of music emerging in the 1950s. "This was a problem because Fried had to revamp his image. He needed a new catchphrase, and that's when he decided to use an African-American slang phrase for sex."

xref.title: Support for Moondog's Lawsuit
xref.body: Big band leader Benny Goodman assisted Moondog (Louis Hardin Jr.) in his lawsuit against disc jockey Allan Freed for the unauthorized use of the "Moon Dog" name. His support was instrumental in Moondog winning the case and securing damages and a promise from Freed to cease using the name. "so with the help of big band leader Benny Goodman, he sued Alan Fried, and he won six thousand dollars in damages."

srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 1

xref.title: The Moondog and Pioneering Rock Concerts
xref.body: Alan Freed achieved considerable fame, adopting the moniker "the Moondog" because his radio program aired after midnight. He subsequently began promoting live shows for the artists featured on these R&B records, naming these events "Moondog Balls." These concerts are historically recognized as the first-ever rock concerts. "And looking back, these were the first ever rock concerts."
